patient.chief_complaint: Six-week progressive weakness predominantly proximal lower extremities, preceded by bronchitis, with absent knee and ankle reflexes.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. V. is a 54-year-old woman with end-stage liver disease secondary to primary biliary cholangitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and remote splenectomy presenting with a 6-week history of progressive weakness. She had an episode of bronchitis approximately 7 weeks ago requiring a short course of antibiotics. One week after the bronchitis resolved, she began noticing difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. The weakness has been primarily proximal and lower extremity-predominant. She denies any sensory symptoms, pain, or difficulty with sphincters. She has no diplopia or dysphagia. She denies alcohol use. Her atorvastatin was continued throughout. Her husband noted she seemed more confused than her baseline mild hepatic encephalopathy, though ammonia is not significantly elevated. The 6-week duration initially suggested chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy or a myopathic process. However, the onset was clearly preceded by an acute infectious event, she has areflexia in the lower extremities with preserved upper extremity reflexes, and the progression, while relatively slow for classic GBS, falls within the 4-week range required for the diagnosis. The statin use and proximal weakness pattern, combined with the liver disease and elevated muscle enzymes, created significant diagnostic uncertainty between inflammatory myopathy, statin-induced myopathy, and GBS.

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral peroneal and tibial motor nerves, with reduced CMAP amplitudes; borderline changes in median motor nerves. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally (peroneal); prolonged F-wave latency in bilateral median nerves (56 ms). 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. EMG: neurogenic motor unit changes in lower extremity muscles; short-duration polyphasic units in proximal muscles also noted. Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal involvement. Mixed neurogenic and possible myopathic EMG features. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP (post-bronchitis), with concurrent PBC-associated mitochondrial myopathy explaining elevated CK

differential.key_features: Atorvastatin use with elevated CK — but NCS shows demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy; statin myopathy does not cause areflexia
AMA-positive myopathy known in PBC — but NCS shows neuropathic pattern; biopsy showed limited necrosis not explaining weakness
6-week duration approaches CIDP — but acute onset post-infection and progressive course without relapse favor GBS
End-stage liver disease can cause muscle wasting — but areflexia and demyelinating NCS are not features of hepatic myopathy

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with concurrent myopathic changes

optimal_actions.action: Labs including CK, LFTs, INR, AMA
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Elevated CK and AMA — but NCS confirms GBS not primary myopathy

optimal_actions.action: Lumbar puncture (after INR correction with FFP)

critical_actions: Recognize GBS despite elevated CK — CK is rarely elevated in GBS but does not exclude the diagnosis; NCS pattern (demyelinating, absent F-waves, absent H-reflex) is decisive
Correct coagulopathy (INR 1.9) with FFP before LP — thrombocytopenia also requires assessment
Use non-sucrose IVIG formulation to avoid sucrose nephropathy in this patient with hepatic/renal vulnerability
Hold atorvastatin — eliminate statin contribution to elevated CK
Serial respiratory monitoring — dual restriction from liver disease and GBS
contraindicated_actions: Succinylcholine for RSI if intubation required — use rocuronium
key_reasoning_points: Elevated CK in GBS is rare but documented — elevated CK does NOT exclude GBS; the NCS/EMG pattern is the gold standard
PBC-associated AMA M2 antibodies can mediate direct muscle injury — explains the elevated CK and myoglobin, not the weakness
The angulated fibers on biopsy (if performed) reflect neurogenic atrophy from GBS, not primary myopathy
6-week duration is at the upper boundary for GBS (defined as <4 weeks to nadir) — but onset post-infection and progressive course favor GBS over CIDP
Coagulopathy in liver disease requires INR correction before LP — this is a modifiable risk; do not forego LP

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest primary myopathy (statin-induced or PBC-associated) rather than GBS
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Elevated CK in GBS is rare but occurs; PBC-associated mitochondrial myopathy explains the elevated muscle enzymes; NCS/EMG demyelinating pattern confirms GBS as primary diagnosis

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest statin-induced myopathy as cause of proximal weakness and elevated CK
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Statin myopathy does not cause areflexia or demyelinating NCS changes; statin should be held but is not the primary diagnosis
